unranked_auxiliary_passages.source_heading: Section 2 — Euclidean space and closed balls
unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: This section records basic notation that we will use throughout the paper. To this end, the symbol $\mathbb R^d$ will denote a Euclidean space with inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and the induced norm $\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$. The symbol $B$ will stand for the closed unit ball in $\mathbb R^d$, while $B_r(x)$ will denote the closed ball of radius $r$ around a point $x$.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.note: The localization balls in Theorem 3.1 and the active-manifold definition are closed. Matrix transpose, ordinary Jacobian, operator norm, rank, kernel and orthogonal complements retain their ambient finite-dimensional meanings.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.source_heading: Section 2 — extended-real functions and lower semicontinuity
unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original:
For any function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, the domain, graph, and epigraph are defined as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{dom}f&:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:f(x)<\infty\},\\
\operatorname{gph}f&:=\{(x,f(x))\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R:x\in\operatorname{dom}f\},\\
\operatorname{epi}f&:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R:r\ge f(x)\},
\end{aligned}
\]
respectively. We say that $f$ is closed if $\operatorname{epi}f$ is a closed set, or equivalently if $f$ is lower-semicontinuous.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.note: The effective domain of the scalar extended-real f differs from the nonempty-value domain of the set-valued F. Theorem 3.2 uses lower semicontinuity of its finite nonnegative loss; symmetric and quasiconvex have their standard meanings.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: The symbol $o(h)$ stands for any function $o(\cdot)$ satisfying $o(h)/h\to0$ as $h\searrow0$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.note: This convention resolves the distance remainder in Assumption E and first-order subdifferential approximations; it is not a fixed universal function or a uniform stochastic convergence claim.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Note that for $C^p$ manifolds $\mathcal M$ with $p\ge1$, the projection $P_{\mathcal M}$ is $C^{p-1}$-smooth on a neighborhood of each point $x$ in $\mathcal M$ and is $C^p$-smooth on a neighborhood of the origin in the tangent space $T_{\mathcal M}(x)$ [25]. Moreover, the inclusion $\operatorname{range}(\nabla P_{\mathcal M}(x))\subseteq T_{\mathcal M}(P_{\mathcal M}(x))$ holds for all $x$ near $\mathcal M$ and the equality $\nabla P_{\mathcal M}(x)=P_{T_{\mathcal M}(x)}$ holds for all $x\in\mathcal M$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.note: Records the source local-projection convention needed in Assumption E. The quoted assertion includes p=1 and uses derivatives in the next sentence without a new regularity qualifier; it is retained as source wording, not certified for that endpoint. Do not assume global single-valued projection or silently strengthen p.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: Let $\mathcal M\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a $C^p$-manifold for some $p\ge1$. Then a function $f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R$ is called $C^p$-smooth around a point $x\in\mathcal M$ if there exists a $C^p$ function $\widehat f:U\to\mathbb R$ defined on an open neighborhood $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ of $x$ and that agrees with $f$ on $U\cap\mathcal M$.
unranked_auxiliary_passages.note: This source convention resolves the smoothness clause of Definition 2.1 and the extension selected in Theorem 2.7. The latter explicitly quantifies over any suitable Cp+1 extension and full-rank defining equations.

The dagger in Theorems 2.7 and 5.1 has this meaning. A projected ambient matrix may be singular in normal directions while nonsingular on the tangent subspace; it is not an ordinary ambient inverse. No other hypothesis of Example 2.2 is imported.

unranked_auxiliary_passages.source_heading: Before Assumption C — local smoothness convention
unranked_auxiliary_passages.statement_original: We will assume that in a certain sense, the problem (4.1) is “variationally smooth”. That is, there exists a distinguished manifold $\mathcal M$—the active manifold in concrete examples—containing $\bar x$ and such that the map $x\mapsto P_{T_{\mathcal M}(x)}F(x)$ is single-valued and $C^1$-smooth on $\mathcal M$ near $\bar x$. The following assumption makes this precise.

source_issues: The pinned source is arXiv:2301.06632v1, dated 16 January 2023, 47 PDF pages. Main text and references end after [37] on page 26, before the lettered Appendix A heading. Only the upper reference region of page 26 is retained; appendix bodies are excluded.

Exactly four main-text environments are printed as Theorem: 2.7, 3.1, 3.2 and 5.1. Numbered Propositions, Corollaries, Lemmas, examples, proof citations and introductory restatements are not extra inventoried theorems.

The complete bodies include the unique multiplier and equivalence in Theorem 2.7, both radius bounds and the random Lipschitz-Jacobian condition in Theorem 3.1, the ordered local minimax limits in Theorem 3.2, and all five assumptions plus the final pseudoinverse formula in Theorem 5.1.

Definition 2.6 locates smooth invertibility at (x-bar,v-bar) in the graph of F. Theorem 2.7 and Assumption A instead print (0,x-bar). Theorem 3.1 explicitly localizes the inverse graph, and Theorem 5.1 prints (x-bar,0). The reversed order is preserved, not silently corrected.

Theorem 2.7 assumes a regular subgradient -A(x-bar) in the Frechet subdifferential, while its set-valued map uses the limiting subdifferential. These are distinct notions, and function-value convergence is essential in the limiting definition.
Definition 2.1 localizes the sharpness condition in position and function value, not just a ball. Its tilted version names bar-v but writes v in f_v(x)=f(x)-<v,x>; that mismatch is retained.

Theorem 2.7 uses the calligraphic H built from A, the extension of f and the multiplier. This is not the arbitrary set-valued H in the Section 3 population inclusion. Each is resolved in its own scope.

The embedded-manifold definition supplies surjective Jacobians for local defining equations. The theorem does not assume its projected Sigma is invertible on the full ambient space: nonsingularity is on the tangent space and the result uses a Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse.

The covariant-Jacobian paragraph prints an extension with codomain R^d although the original map has codomain R^m. It also omits explicit Cp smoothness of the extension in that sentence and alternates nabla F and nabla_M F. The scalar extension definition preceding it is explicit; the vector wording is retained with its issues.

Theorem 3.1 inherits Assumptions A and B and additionally requires a square-integrable random Lipschitz bound on the Jacobian, a measurable solution selection, and probability tending to one of staying in the specified local ball. Solution existence and local convergence are not guaranteed by definition of SAA.

The radius bounds in Theorem 3.1 contain E L and lip(sigma)^(-1). Zero denominators or degenerate constant local inverses are not assigned extra conventions in the main text. The norm in (3.3) has no operator-norm subscript, unlike the second Jacobian moment in Assumption B.

The paragraph before Theorem 3.1 prints Cov(M(x-bar,z)) although the model and the theorem use A. No object M is introduced there. The theorem original retains A; the background typo is not promoted to an extra interface.

Theorem 3.2 assumes only A and B, not Theorem 3.1 or its Lipschitz-Jacobian condition. Its loss is any symmetric, quasiconvex, lower semicontinuous nonnegative finite function. Its estimator is unrestricted apart from the printed mapping; no SAA algorithm requirement is inserted.

The phi-divergence paragraph requires a convex C3 phi on (0,infinity) with phi(1)=0. It does not print positive second derivative, a first-derivative normalization, or conventions for zero densities and singular laws. For example, the printed class includes degenerate phi; source review preserves the stated class without certifying the lower-bound theorem for each member.

The admissible neighborhood requires existence of a perturbed solution in U, using the local neighborhood from the preceding assumptions. It does not explicitly give uniqueness or a measurable selection of these perturbed centers. This is recorded rather than resolved using the excluded proof.

Assumption C describes a local tangent reduction of an abstract inclusion. Preceding prose supplies C1 smoothness and x-bar in the manifold, while the displayed clauses do not explicitly impose Cp smoothness of F_M. The Cp inverse conclusion in Theorem 5.1 is preserved with that regularity issue, not repaired.

Assumption E1 subtracts the set-valued F(P_M(x)) before tangent projection. Assumption C1 gives a single projected value, explaining the intended tangent comparison; no norm convention for an arbitrary set is invented. E2 has a squared noise factor multiplying both its little-o term and C alpha.
Assumptions D and E use a calligraphic neighborhood U and U_F; Assumption J uses an ordinary matrix U. They are different objects despite text extraction rendering them with the same letter.
The generalized-update paragraph says noise assumptions will be given in Section 6, while the actual assumptions are in Section 5. The forward reference is retained as printed.

Assumption I prints sublabels J1-J4. It requires a strict conditional fourth-moment bound and permits gamma=1. Theorem 5.1 separately restricts gamma to (1/2,1) and assumes almost-sure convergence of the iterates; it does not prove global convergence.

Assumption J says the columns of U form an orthogonal basis, not an orthonormal basis. It defines Sigma through the Gaussian limit of sums of U-transpose nu^(1), so Sigma is in tangent coordinates. Theorem 5.1 multiplies Sigma directly by ambient Jacobians without a coordinate transformation; the displayed covariance can be dimensionally incompatible. No U factors or orthonormality assumptions are silently inserted.

Theorem 5.1 applies to the abstract generalized update. The active-manifold, subgradient, forward-backward and specific stochastic variational-inequality examples provide sufficient-condition results but are not additional hypotheses of this theorem.

Gaussian laws, conditional expectation, covariance, convergence in distribution, almost-sure convergence, independent sampling, measurable selections, operator norms, symmetric quasiconvex losses and Radon-Nikodym derivatives remain stated ambient mathematical prerequisites. Source review verifies transcription and dependencies, not the correctness of the proofs or of the recorded source assertions.

2.7.common: Cp A, subdifferential continuity, Cp+1 active manifold at a regular subgradient, and chosen smooth defining equations and extension.
2.7.equivalence: Smooth inverse exists if and only if the projected Jacobian is nonsingular on the tangent space; the derivative is its pseudoinverse.

3.1.additional: Random square-integrable Lipschitz-Jacobian bound, both radius bounds, measurable empirical solution, probability of local membership tending to one.

3.2.loss: Symmetric, quasiconvex, lower semicontinuous, finite and nonnegative.
3.2.limit_order: c to infinity, then liminf in k, with supremum over laws in B_(c/k).

5.1.additional: gamma strictly between 1/2 and 1; almost-sure convergence to the fixed solution; positive tangent coercivity.
5.1.conclusion: Smooth inverse and normal limit of the average iterate; pseudoinverse derivative formula.
